name: Scalewoven Creature (CR +2)
body:
While their behavior is most of the time wholly uninteresting, they have two crucial qualities that make them both unique and incredibly dangerous.

The first of these is their sheer invulnerability. Scaleweavers resemble ticks, but their bodies are covered in plates of material that’s organic in nature, but rivaling or possibly exceeding adamantine in toughness. This armor is layered and interwoven so seamlessly that it’s a wonder that the creature is able to crawl and climb despite being covered in such a tight shell. This armor blunts physical trauma and scaleweavers are impervious to acid, temperature extremes, biological agents and seemingly even the passage of time itself. They eat ravenously when they can, but they can remain inactive and without food for hundreds of years, or maybe more.

Seemingly the only force of nature that can harm a scaleweaver is electricity, and even then, only in the amounts found in a lightning bolt and greater. Of course, being wholly mundane creatures, more esoteric ways of extermination, such as negative energy and disintegration, are fully effective in killing the creatures.

The second element inherent to their danger stems from their method of killing. They bite into the target with uncountable miniscule, incredibly sharp teeth and adhere to its skin with a poorly understood substance they can rapidly excrete from their bodies. While that would be dangerous enough considering how hard they are to kill, the poison they then pump into the prey’s bloodstream is the most terrifying part and their true way of killing. The poison is almost akin to acid with how fast and devastatingly it acts. It somehow breaks down the target’s very form, disassembling it into a biotic sludge. While dangerous enough in small doses, the sight of a whole swarm injecting their poison into a living creature is the true stuff of nightmares, with the whole body rapidly melting down into a pool of vaguely fleshy goo, which the creatures then proceed to ravenously consume.

While scaleweavers are unrivaled in the insect world in terms of both defensive and offensive capabilities, they are both quite slow and rarely tenacious in pursuit. As such, general alertness and caution go a long way in avoiding the terrible fate of falling prey to those creatures. Engaging those beings in combat is ill advised, although their favored place of habitation is often also the favored place of exploration for intrepid adventurers, and even though the prospect of both agonizing and absolute body obliteration might put a stop to some of such heroes, most are either too sure of themselves or plain too unwise not to probe the place for treasure or even a greater evil to put down.

With their poison numbering among the most dangerous, supernatural or not, across the planes, their armor putting even the greatest metals to shame and the adhesive they create being a mundane alternative to sovereign glue, many scholars are keen to study scaleweavers. Fortunately, colonies of those creatures are hard to come by, with volunteers to capture them being even more scarce. The facts that the liquids produced by scaleweavers dry out and lose potency almost instantly or that you can’t really forge chitin-like material are only a small deterrent, and there are always rumors of experimental alchemical treatments or reshaping the armor with magic.

An average scaleweaver is the color of burnished gold and 4 to 6 inches long, but they can grow up to a foot if well fed and venerable enough. According to some legends, truly ancient scaleweavers living in the deepest, evil and magic rich caverns can grow many times larger, presenting a whole other level of terror.

Creating a Scalewoven Creature

“Scalewoven” is an acquired template that can be added to any living creature (referred to hereafter as the base creature).

A Scalewoven creature uses all the base creature’s statistics and special abilities except as noted here.

Challenge Rating: Same as base creature +2.

Defensive Abilities: A Scalewoven creature gains DR 10/—; fast healing 1; acid, cold and fire resistance 10 and the ferocity special ability.

Special Attacks: A Scalewoven creature gains the ability to rage as a barbarian of a level equal to half its hit dice (minimum 1). After the rage ends, the Scalewoven Creature is wracked with agonizing, debilitating pain that imposes a –4 penalty on attack rolls, skill checks, and ability checks. Each round as a free action, the creature can make a DC 25 Will save to ignore those penalties for the round. The pain lasts for twice the number of rounds that the Scalewoven creature spent in the rage.

Special Qualities: A Scalewoven creature gains the following special quality:

Living Carapace (Ex)

Scaleweavers covering the creature function, for the most part, as a suit of masterwork full plate armor. The wearer gains a +9 armor bonus with a Max Dex Bonus of +1 and armor check penalty of -5. The creature can sleep without suffering any fatigue, despite sleeping in heavy armor. The living carapace is not made of metal, and as such can be worn by druids without penalty. The living carapace has hardness 20 and 60 hp and repairs itself at a rate of 1 hit point per hour. Living carapace cannot be targeted by any effects that target objects, as it is composed of living creatures, but it can be sundered or targeted with damaging effects. If the living carapace gains the broken condition, the Scalewoven creature is afflicted with Scaleweaver Poison (as in the Scaleweaver Swarm statblock). If the living carapace gains the destroyed condition, the creature immediately loses the template and is afflicted with four doses of Scaleweaver Poison.

Weaknesses: A Scalewoven creature gains a temporary negative level when it first gains this template and every 24 hours thereafter. This negative level never becomes permanent and there is no save to resist this effect. The negative level can be safely removed (for example with a Restoration spell) and comes back at the usual time.

Abilities: Str +2, Int -2 (minimum 1), Wis -2, Cha -2

For some unclear reasons, scaleweavers occasionally don’t attack creatures they meet. In those extremely rare cases, scaleweavers still crawl onto the creature, cling to it using their natural adhesive and bite into its skin. The difference is, in these cases they do it gently, not tearing the flesh and not injecting poison. Creatures unaware of what these beings are often try to remove them, only to realize it’s not possible without tearing the skin, as its adhesive and dozens of tiny teeth are too strong. If the creature somehow manages to destroy some, they inject their lethal poison and the process ends. If left on the body, they enter a symbiotic relationship with their host. If only a few scaleweavers have done that, the only effects are constant pain, increased aggression and a small degree of protection (represented as a bonus to natural armor). They soon begin to multiply, covering the wearer’s body in an impenetrable, living shell, similar to a suit of adamantine armor. This process is the genesis of their name, as they act as scales in the armor they weave across their host’s body. Specialized mask, guards and bracelets have to be employed so the scaleweavers don’t cover the host’s face and joints. Such a set has to be deliberately created for the task and costs at least 5000 gold pieces for a medium humanoid and possibly more for creatures that are larger or possessed of atypical anatomy.

It is not known how scaleweavers choose their hosts. Two leading theories are that they target either creatures wielding some degree of innate magical power or those of incredible evil. With scaleweavers not observed to have any ways of detecting neither magic nor evil, there is only anecdotal evidence to support those theories, major of which being, of course, their favorite habitat.

The scaleweavers feed on small amounts of host’s blood, and some say his very soul. In return, they pump enzymes into its bloodstream, allowing for bursts of adrenaline-fueled rage and unrivaled tenacity. Those substances also greatly increase the healing rate of the host creature, making its wounds heal almost on the spot. Other than general weakness from scaleweaver’s feeding, the host has to endure near constant pain, which strains its mental faculties and makes clear thinking nearly impossible. The pain gets much worse if the creature allows itself to drift off into a state of scaleweaver-enhanced fury, but fortunately has seemingly no other long-term effects. Of course, scaleweavers are hard to remove and harder to destroy, and breaking the symbiotic cycle inevitably causes them to pump their devastating poison directly into their host’s body, making sure their newly unwilling partner won’t grace the world much longer.

Despite these dangers, there are multiple ways to safely remove scaleweavers. The most straightforward option is sundering the carapace, taking care to protect the creature against poison. Another option is casting the freedom spell on the creature (which is entitled to a Will save if it is unwilling). This unfortunately creates a scaleweaver swarm 1d3 rounds later, when the creatures come to their senses after this event. Of course, many other methods may exist, although cases of Scalewoven are rare enough that not many of them have been properly tested.
